question: Does indexing a collection, or downloading through it, make a first visit to a directory materially slower than the same first visit on a daemon that is idle and fully indexed?
why_now: The row says 'responsive navigation during initial indexing and competing downloads' and names no number, and the code's only bound is a sixty-second give-up deadline. So 'responsive' cannot be failed. live-navigation-during-indexing.json measured the case properly and said as much in its own decision rule -- 'the box is not tickable on this evidence whatever the numbers' -- and it was right: it had good figures and nothing to hold them against. What is missing is not another measurement but a question that can come out wrong.
why_a_ratio_and_not_a_latency: An absolute bar on a first visit measures the provider and the network, which this project does not control and which differ on every machine. The row is about interference: the clause is 'during initial indexing and competing downloads', and the failure it names is the daemon's own work getting in the way of the user's. A ratio against an idle control on the same machine, the same network and the same collection removes everything that is not that.
registration_honesty: One arm's answer is already known and this registration cannot pretend otherwise: the competing-download factor on p95 was measured at 1.37 and replicated at 1.36. The INDEXING factor is unknown, because the idle control has never been run -- every previous run measured during indexing and had nothing to compare against. The bound below is therefore set for a number nobody has seen, and the download arm is carried along as a check that the method reproduces what it already produced.

arms.idle: The collection fully indexed, nothing downloading, the daemon quiet. First visits to directories not previously listed.
arms.indexing: The same, while the collection is being indexed from nothing.
arms.indexing_and_download: The same again, with a large file being read through the mount.

endpoint: p95 of a first-visit listing in each arm, and the ratio of each to the idle arm. At least 50 previously unvisited directories per arm, on one machine, one network and one collection, within one session.

predictions.P1: Every arm reaches at least 50 first visits and no listing fails, or the run measures nothing and says so.
predictions.P2: The indexing arm's p95 is under twice the idle arm's. Two, because that is where the daemon's own work has stopped being a background cost and become half of what the user is waiting for.
predictions.P3: The download arm's p95 is under twice the idle arm's as well, and its ratio against the indexing arm reproduces the 1.36-1.37 already measured, within the spread of those two runs.
predictions.P4: No single listing in any arm exceeds five seconds. The tail is what a person calls a freeze, and a percentile cannot see it. Five, because the existing maximum across two runs is 1,184.9 ms and a bound four times that is loose enough to be about freezes rather than about slowness.

decision_rule.P2_and_P4_hold: The row's clause is met on the reading that can be failed: the daemon's own work is a background cost rather than the thing the user waits for. The row can be ticked, naming this endpoint rather than an absolute latency.
decision_rule.P2_fails: Indexing is the cost. That is a real finding and a fixable one -- it is contention inside this project, not the provider -- and the row stays open with a number attached.
decision_rule.P4_fails: A freeze happened. That outranks every percentile in this artifact and the row stays open regardless of the ratios.
decision_rule.P3_fails_alone: The method did not reproduce a figure it has produced twice. Then the run says nothing about P2 either, and is repeated rather than interpreted.

what_this_does_not_cover: One machine, one network, one collection of 184,000 items. A ratio removes the provider from the comparison; it does not make the result portable to a collection ten times the size.

result.where: The Fedora VM, the owner's real drive, 184,076 items, a cold engine of the validator's own beside the machine's running daemon. scripts/vm/run.sh fedora; cirrove validate-onedrive-navigation --per-arm 60 --idle-seconds 600.
three_runs_and_two_fixture_defects: First attempt: the three arms shared one directory tree and the first two ate it -- 406 samples indexing, 1,142 with a download, and the collection's 1,548 directories were gone, leaving the control arm two samples. Indexing also finished part way through the second arm, so 292 of its samples were served from the index (p50 4.4 ms against 205 ms for the arm before it), which is a different measurement wearing the same label. VOID. Each arm now takes a budget of samples rather than a slice of time.

Second attempt, one download stream: all three arms clean at 60 samples, and the download arm's p95 came out BELOW the indexing arm's -- 264 ms against 315, a factor of 0.84 where two earlier runs had measured 1.36 and 1.37. The arm's only claim to be competing was its name. The validator now counts the bytes the competing transfer moves: 50.2 MB at 1.75 MiB/s. A transfer at a sixth of the bandwidth the host runs had is not the same condition.
Third attempt, six streams: 220.0 MB at 7.79 MiB/s, and the interference came back -- p95 274.1 ms alone against 335.8 ms competing, a factor of 1.23.

verdict.P1: HOLDS. Sixty first visits in each of the three arms, no listing failed, and the indexing arms were entirely inside the index build.
verdict.P2: FAILS as written, by a factor of sixteen -- and the prediction was the thing at fault. I asked for the indexing arm's p95 to be under twice the idle arm's. They are 274 ms and 8.4 ms, and they are not two measurements of one thing: during the index build a first visit is a provider round trip, and once the build is done the same visit is a read of the local index and never reaches the provider at all. The ratio is a statement about where the answer comes from, not about the daemon's own work getting in the way. It should never have been the bound.
verdict.P3: FAILS, and the failure is about the method rather than the daemon. The download arm's p95 is 40 times the idle arm's, for the same reason P2 fails. Its ratio against the INDEXING arm -- both provider-bound, differing only in whether something else is pulling bytes, which is the comparison the clause is actually about -- is 1.23 against the 1.36 and 1.37 measured twice before. Close, same direction, outside the stated spread. The cause is measured: at one stream the competing transfer moved 1.75 MiB/s and the factor was 0.84, at six it moved 7.79 MiB/s and the factor was 1.23. Interference scales with what the transfer actually takes, and no earlier run recorded that -- so 1.36 and 1.37 were never reproducible figures, because the condition they were measured under was not written down.
verdict.P4: HOLDS. The slowest listing in any arm was 486 ms, against a ceiling of five seconds, and nothing exceeded 500 ms in either indexing arm.

decision: The row stays open, by this artifact's own rule: P3 did not reproduce, so the run is repeated rather than interpreted, and two of the three runs here were the repeats. What it has produced is worth more than a tick. The clause now has a control arm for the first time -- a settled daemon answers a first visit in 5.4 ms at the median, a building one in 179 ms, and the difference is the index, not contention. It has an interference figure with the condition recorded beside it. And it has the reason the earlier figures could not be reproduced: nobody had written down what the competing transfer was moving.
what_would_close_it: A registration whose bounds can fail for the right reason: an absolute ceiling on a first visit during the index build (p95 under 500 ms, no listing over five seconds, no failures), and an interference factor measured against a competing transfer whose rate is declared in advance and recorded in the result. Both are met by the numbers here; neither was what this artifact asked for, and rewriting the question after seeing the answer is the one thing a registration exists to prevent.
